body: Pioneer of global investing. Folklore-grade but widely repeated: in Sept 1939, at the outbreak of WWII, he borrowed $10,000 and bought 100 shares of every NYSE stock trading under $1 (~104 companies, ~34 in bankruptcy) and sold ~4 years later for roughly 4x (details unverified in this research). Templeton Growth Fund (1954-1992): $10,000 grew to ~$2m by 1992, ~13.96% annualised per one source (14.5% often quoted, unverified). Structural edge: early access to cheap foreign markets - he bought Japan in the 1960s at P/E ~3-4x when few Westerners did. Process: 'the time of maximum pessimism is the best time to buy'; compare price with value across every country and industry; buy the cheapest relative to long-term earnings power; diversify widely. His cycle line: 'bull markets are born on pessimism, grow on skepticism, mature on optimism and die on euphoria.' Mistakes: exited Japan years before its 1989 peak (early, missed the final leg); a diversified value approach lags in growth-led eras. 1999-2000 he reportedly shorted Nasdaq IPOs around lock-up expiries (unverified). Copyable: keep a global/sector 'cheapest vs own history' list and act when news is worst; diversify bargain baskets rather than betting on one distressed name; use his pessimism-to-euphoria ladder as a cycle checklist.
title: John Templeton - global bargain hunting at maximum pessimism
